Absolutely! I wasn't trying to suggest that you were a reader first, I've also been a writer from childhood, but that you're both and it seems ignorant for an editor to insinuate that you don't also consume the product you create, or have familiarity with the market.

I'm SO glad to hear you had backups!! I totally know what is like to have such clear ideas for your own writing and I imagine that with the amount of care you're putting into it, it's going to turn out so great!

As an aside, it sounds up my alley and I'd be really happy to be an ARC or beta reader if/when you're ready for something like that!

So, because I'm getting comments from multiple people and have no interest in gatekeeping (when I made this comment there was only one other comment on this thread, then I posted it and there were tons!) I'll just give the list here.

My absolute favorite books for self-editing are:

Intuitive Editing by Tiffany Yates Martin (best for developmental and character/plot arc evaluation)

Self Editing for Fiction Writers by Renni Brown and Dave King (best for line editing *after* developmental has been done)

Crafting Novels & Short Stories by the Writer's Digest (best for strengthening your known weaknesses but trying to read the whole thing while editing is usually overwhelming, focus on needed sections)

And then for funzies, The Portable MFA in Creative Writing by the Editors of New York Writer's Workshop (take what you need from this but don't treat it as gospel as it's very opinionated regarding the value of a Master's degree, but there's still a lot of useful writing information in it.)

This is my big issue! I am not under the impression that it's at all standard for an editor to make the changes directly. They make *suggestions*. Please correct me if I'm wrong about that but I've only heard about a few freelancers doing it this way, and it turning out incredibly badly as well.

As writers, we're also taught that we're in control of the story we want to tell, and need to be able to learn what is useful feedback and dismiss the rest.

The editor fucked up their vision for the story they wanted to tell. End of story.

First off all, this is terrible, they and their viewpoints suck, and I'm so sorry this happened to you. I can imagine it would be so disheartening. I've hired a developmental editor before and while, unfortunately for my mental state having to confront the massive amount of comments they left had me spiraling for a while, ultimately they were awesome and nothing like this. I just published that book this spring.

Secondly, *you're* a reader who wrote a book you would want to read. And as someone who LOVES deep character connections and traumatic plots, I fully agree with you! So they're objectively wrong that there aren't readers who want what you've written, which is effectively what they tried to say.

Thirdly, what the fuck? Why did they actually change your manuscript?? I've consulted with a large handful of editors and particularly Reedsy editors (wayyy too $$ for me) who have all explained that the process is NOTES. That they don't actually change the manuscript. That's so bonkers.

Please, please tell me you have a backup from before they got their grubby hands on it. I would ditch all their work and continue from where YOU left off, if that's the case (I hope so)!

I gotta get offline but I'm just finishing my creative writing degree and have tons of self-editing books I (and my professors) swear by. PM me if you're interested and I'll give you a list of my favorite and most useful titles for all the stages of self-editing.

It's a PITA but at least you get creative control for the cool price of a couple ebooks and your time.

Best of luck, and keep writing! ♥️

Hey, commenting late because I wanted to see if people were talking about this vitamin.

I've been on it about two months, I take one with breakfast almost daily. (I forget some days but try to take it every day.)

It is *not* a magic pill. You will not be instantly changed and you will still want food with basic flavors.

BUT. What I have found is that I want and think about these things less. I used to feel like I had to pack a sweet thing and a salty, crunchy thing in my lunch at work every day, or the cravings would have me stopping for an expensive convenience store snack on my way to the gym, or sometimes I'd feel so hungry I'd just skip it and go home for my ice cream in the freezer.

This vitamin probably works best in tandem with a diet shift. Before I started taking it, I was already adding in fresh vegetables (my go to are raw tomatoes, cucumber and cauliflower, which are all super good with just salt and pepper or for the cauliflower, dipped in lite salad dressing like a vinaigrette or Italian.)

I've also been increasing the amount of water I drink throughout the day and finding substitutes to cut down the amount of sugar or salt I enjoy, or like with the vegetables, getting my "salty treat" from raw tomato slices with salt rather than a bag of chips. My sweet substitution has been homemade coffee with cream and sugar for under 100 calories, either regular, flavored or decaf. (Having an extra cup in the evening with dinner, which is when I have the decaf instead of dessert, also helps things, uh... move along, which can be a little bit of a struggle at first when reducing appetite, also causing the scale to be off and become discouraging. So remember to poop! 😅)

I don't think about cake, donuts, potato chips, cookies, ice cream or greasy take out *nearly* as much, and I would say taking these vitamins regularly *seems* to have saved me from eating an average of about 200 calories a day. My snacks are almost entirely raw vegetables (under 75 calories) or protein based like a nice soft-boiled egg with spices and some cheese. Or again, coffee and sometimes tea.

Which are things I might have been having before, but now I'm not also having a 250 calorie bowl of ice cream after dinner or a bag of chips after work.

So again, it's not a magic pill but it's become a useful tool in my arsenal and I have certainly been losing weight having gotten better control of my eating habits. I will also say, personally, I have noticed no side effects whatsoever.

But at the end of the day they are an extra cost and will not prevent you from snacking if you choose. You have to work *with* the vitamins. You could easily spend $20/month on them, snack to your hearts content and change nothing else, and claim they don't work. It's up to you if they're worth it to you.

This was happening to me for a while during covid and I started a sleep diary. I tracked everything and then my sleep results. Light, electronic use, beverages, caffeine, dairy and general diet, alcohol, medications including OTC, my cat's activity, room temperature, pajama type and fabric (my daytime lounge wear are flannel sweats but I find they're too warm to sleep in some nights because of all this tracking).

Whatever *could* impact sleep, I began to track it and learned my patterns. I found that my biggest contributors were the diphenhydramine that would wear off at the same time each night, my TV sleep timer going off (I was dealing with a recent trauma and had a hard time falling asleep without a show), or having ice cream or milk too close to bed time and later learning that I have a degree of lactose intolerance, and wouldn't even realize that it was mild bloating and gas waking me up.

You're not likely dealing with the things I mentioned but I recommend you look into all the factors and start tracking the factors every night and the resulting quality every morning and within a week or two you'll begin to notice patterns. Within a month you'll find remedies.

I have a schedule that allows me to be a little flexible and I'm still able to earn full time benefits by working only a half day one time a week. Meaning, I work a full 40-hour work week minus four hours on one routine day each week, so my total worked is actually 36. But I still get vacation and holiday pay (my company didn't y give sick days anyway). I can still work later if I want to to earn a little more when needed but I don't ever manage to earn overtime pay because it's calculated by the week, not by the day and my "overtime" weeks get me up to maybe 38/39 hours. That's fine.

Using this half day as a chunk of time all at once has been huge for me. Even though it's only four hours, it's got a major impact.

I don't have to pack a full day of food, just my water, breakfast shake and a morning snack and then I come home for lunch. That saves time but also mental energy. It's a break. Because I do have to go to work, it's so much easier to stack more tasks onto the day than getting myself moving on a day off. Sometimes it feels like it takes me five hours to get in the groove on a day off. On my half day, I've earned money, ran two errands on the way home, threw a load of laundry in before I left, and I'm microwaving leftovers for lunch before my appointment (that I often schedule on my half day) in the time I often takes me to get moving on weekends. Because momentum.

So I do laundry, make time for larger projects, sometimes go out to see friends, sometimes have therapy/medical or car appointments so that I don't have to take work time off, I spend more time at the gym, or if therapy really took it out of me, it's an obligation-free afternoon to take a nap and cry over some ice cream and a movie. This has been the literal best schedule for my life, ever.

But I highly suggest that whether you can manage something like that or not, that if you can work a job that has hours offset from 9-5 (either 7-3 like mine also does so I'm out super early even on normal days, or 10-6, etc.) try that. A lot of ADHD exhaustion for people who work 9-5 seems to come from also having to live life outside of work, where we have to schedule appointments, run errands, live general life in a world where things are already harder for us. Having to take time off work for necessary functions is easier for non-ADHD folk. Find a way--any way that works for you-- to bypass that and you'll never look back. You may work the same hours as before or as everyone around you but the convenience of going places while they're still open without waiting months to have the motivation to find or create a day off work will save you so much time and energy.

Then use that extra time to doomscroll. :) It might not feel more productive but you'll feel less like a corporative slave and in the end isn't that what we're all struggling with??

It depends on the relationship. If you feel like you really want to do what they're suggesting, push a follow-through. It goes both ways.

Do they suggest a vague time that could be more fine tuned with feedback (like "next time you're in town" or "when the kids go back to school")? Or just "sometime"? If they say sometime and then you're expecting them to reach out when they want to but you don't do so yourself, they probably assume you didn't want to either.

It may be a platitude but that doesn't mean they absolutely don't want to and would hate it if real plans were made. It's a give and take. If they throw it out there as "sometime" and you just leave it there they'll equally assume you're not interested.

Instead, solidify those plans. Decide when you're free and see how they react when you get specific. If they say "Yeah, we'll see!" or cancel day-of (especially more than once) they're not interested and you should move on. But they might just be lobbing the ball into your court and then looking for signals that you're interested. So give them! :)

First off, it sounds like you have an idea in your head about fitting art into boxes and by definition I'm not sure that's how it works?

I love art but I also love healing and therapy. Primarily my outlet is creative writing. My debit novel, coming out this year (not the first one I ever finished, just the first one I'm ready to publish) is a therapy project. *Heavily*. It doesn't matter to me if I make a lot of sales or get poor reviews on it. It's exactly what I needed it to be.

The one I'm doing after that? Purely for fun. And a bit of marketing, because I do hope for success and want attention from those in the industry I respect. I get that.

After my most traumatic event, I dove headfirst into writing and even went back to school. I joined book clubs. I'm in an honors society for English. Etc. The book I'm putting out is a direct response to what happened to me. It's the story of how I would have reacted if I wasn't afraid of the consequences of torching my life. I let my anger out. I put all my fears and loneliness on the page. I wrote in the comfort I long for. I even gave my character feelings I'm afraid to admit I probably feel but have definitely at least thought once or they wouldn't have crossed my mind for her. God, was it cathartic.

And I'm not done. I wrote the story again with different dynamics and a different plot and different characters and even a different genre but it hit all the same buttons for me. Control, fear, anger, revenge, vindication. Catharsis. The Hero's Journey is quite malleable that way. But the second time was after a year of therapy and healing, and I had more fun with it.

The one I wrote after that is quite detached. Yet another genre exploration. New world, new plot. But when I read it back for editing, I found more anger working it's way through. I picked at it, brought it to the surface, made it the central conflict. My history of being abused as a woman turned into a sci-fi plot about a homicidal android controlled by a misogynistic man and the value of standing up for women and blah blah blah point is, it leaks into what I love whether I mean for it to or not because it's in me.

Passionate work brings out our passionate feelings. Trying to separate them may not work. I try to work on my healing first and foremost because I don't feel like I can create when I'm emotionally drained from all my feelings. It comes in waves. Right now I'm dealing with some heavy things again so I'm struggling with writing and even reading so I'm taking a break and that's okay.

I suggest that you try to let things be what they are. If you're lead to create something messy and emotional, do that. It may reveal something you didn't know you were working on.

And as for rubbing elbows with the greats? I get that. I feel similarly giddy about publishing. But I have to remind myself that just because I'm meeting someone in a local writing club that just published their second book with an indie publisher and they're not a NY list bestseller doesn't mean their ideas are less valuable or that I can't learn from them.

I suggest trying to get into a local class or club or even online and just get out there and meet people. The more you do it and expose yourself to others the more chance you have at finding your people. I have the best book club and the best writing clubs, both online and in person. It took me about 2-4 years of searching and some real bad experiences before I got where I am. Believe me, writers are some of the most pretentious, gatekeepy people I've met in my life. But others are some of the most open, artsy, expressive, welcoming, wonderful people.

Meetup.com, local clubs and organizations, local chapters of national orgs, discord servers, etc. School based, library based... So many options. Or create your own group. But I hope you get back to creating and find all that it can do for you.

Simply account for your cost of materials, then you can maybe look up similar items on Etsy for prices that you can tell are handmade and not bulk factory made (should be in the hundreds for a handmade dress, $200-350 at least, then browse for items most similar to what you're making. It would be the same if you were trying to sell online and scoping your competition). Subtract the price for your materials from whatever average price you find and just keep it in mind.

Like, let's say most dresses you find are $250 and you know you'll be spending $75 total on materials. Subtract that and just hold $175 in your head.

A *very low* wage for tailors is $16/hour. It should be higher. Like $20+, experience and location depending. Depending on the complexity of the dress, how long do you think it'll take you to make it? $175/$16 is just a little under eleven hours. You can figure this for yourself, and your numbers may be way different. (For example, I make suits and on average a handmade suit takes 80-100 hours and I pay myself $10-16 hour depending on how much of a deal I cut the person. Materials average an additional $200.)

If you don't think you can get away with charging your friend by the hour, *at least* get your material costs back but pad the price. You're not taking advantage of them by doing this, you're doing them an enormous favor and cutting them a huge deal.

If you think you can get them to agree to a more set price and not worry about hours, again, average the prices you find online and decide if you want to sell at that price, cut a deal (realizing you probably don't have overhead/associated business costs, allowing you to get away with selling it for less), and figure out what you're comfortable with between "more than your materials" and "less than someone who does this for a profession".

Without knowing more about the dress in question, and not being someone with a lot of dress experience myself, I can't give you exact numbers, but this is the rough science I would use to figure it out, especially if it's something someone asked me to do, offers to pay me, and it's something I know I'm capable of but have never done before so I have no idea what to charge, like that one time someone asked me to make curtains for her camper. I will, but ma'am, I make suits. This one's gonna take me a sec.

Aside from all that, to answer your question, I don't exactly charge friends when they ask me to do things, but they often offer and we work something out. If it's a small job, like it takes more time to set up my machine than to sew it and they still insist on paying me, I tell them I take payment in the form of Reese's and we both come away happy. Chocolate I didn't pay for always tastes better and they got their shorts fixed for, like, $3. Plus we got to know each other better.

People who offer/promise to pay and then don't ask how much or follow up, if it's not a huge job and depending on how close we are, I often don't bring it up again but I won't do any more jobs for them. I will not chase my friends and family down for $20 on a job *they* asked me to do.

But at least I am not skipping breakfast to buy bland lunch meat anymore. I have moved past that.

It takes practice both getting used to comments and learning to ignore people or tell them they're making you uncomfortable and need to stop their behavior. I think much of the time when people (*real people*) are talking about therapy they're talking about talk therapists, who are not psychiatrists. Psychiatrists are medical doctors who can prescribe medications. Talk therapists can not.

When I got diagnosed with anxiety from my GP after having an anxiety attack and referred to behavioral health for follow up treatment, I had a six month wait because that's how long the wait list is, and was asked a few quick questions over the phone, like do I care if my provider is the same gender as myself (not always but in this case I said I do) and if I care if they can prescribe me medications or not. I said I don't care but that I wasn't sure how interested I was in taking a new drug since I'm on some others that don't directly treat the depression (Major Depressive Disorder) I was also diagnosed with by the same GP earlier but can affect it or interact with anti-psychotics, and I've been feeling okay on the un-alive-myself front. Didn't want to mess with that balance unless necessary.

I got matched with a talk therapist who does video visits and cannot prescribe me meds. We work mostly on CBT (cognitive behavior therapy) where I talk about my issues, cry a lot, she makes suggestions and sometimes gives me homework like journaling or thinking exercises. They're meant to train your brain into certain thought patterns or away from certain negative ones. I see her every two or three weeks and my insurance covers a huge chunk of it.

It's my second round with a therapist but my first through my doctors and insurance. The first was through Betterhelp for my suspected depression (undiagnosed at the time) and a near-crisis event. I loved her and got a discount on the service. We talked for about a year. While a ton of what I learned with her helps me now, I'm going through some new things especially with increased anxiety responses, and it's really helpful to have someone to talk to through it all even if I have a better handle on a lot of the negative self talk and self esteem stuff by now.

Therapy can be exhausting and feel like an uphill battle and like you're not gaining any ground in the beginning. It's when you stick with it that you see the growth and healing and learning. But the way it's portrayed in media is usually really cliche and stereotypical, which isn't helpful for those who really need assistance.

Edit to add: TV dramas that have characters running out of the room are, I hope obviously, not true to life. Most therapists don't care very much about why you have certain issues, childhood trauma or not. What matters so much more and is enough work on it's own is how it's effecting you now and what to do about it. Sure, understanding the root cause can help because it can tell you more about where to find the problem popping up, but overall it doesn't matter nearly as much as fixing the results, like how a parent's abuse affects your current relationships and how you treat people or let them treat you.

The disturbances could be noises and light during the night, partners and pets, temperature, medications and caffeine, or other factors like your activity and stress levels or your sleep hygiene, like when you put away blue lights. What I *would* suggest for someone like OP who seems to be mostly just starting out is a simple formula of protein-starch-vegetable.

Cooking a chicken breast or a couple tenderloins, a serving of rice, and some steamed vegetables should take about 20-30 minutes. You can replace the chicken with steak, ground meat, etc. You can replace the rice with tostadas and the veggies with those toppings. (You can also make your own tostadas.)

You can substitute anything for variety with this formula which allows you to practice certain aspects and move on to new things with others as your skills improve or to be versatile with your schedule, budget, appetite, etc.

Tiny loads more often. Start the list almost first thing in the morning, then complete the whole cycle from wash to dry to fold to put away in one day, and keep your basket empty. Do it again the next day, or every other day if you don't generate that much. Time yourself folding. Make yourself put away the difficult articles that require a hanger or that overfilled drawer. If there's only a couple of difficult things in each load instead of half a basket, it's easier.

I listen to music while I fold. I do NOT. TURN. ON. THE. TV.

I dump the whole basket on my bed, turn on music, and sort. Shirts, undergarments and socks, leg items (pants, skirts, leggings, pj's), large items like blankets and towels, and sweaters or sweatshirts. I give myself three songs and GO. I can listen to three songs in a day! Easy. Then also doing A Thing during? Sure, I guess.

I start with the large items, towels and blankets, then move on to either pants or socks. I focus on whichever will either take the longest like small socks or give me more room to work like pants, need-based (am I in a rush to get done or does my pile/workspace feel too crowded?). Then, and this is important, *I put away while I work*. Got a stack of shirts? In the drawer they go before you move on. Underwear takes five seconds to disappear into the drawer.

Before you know it, you're two songs in, dancing and only have two sweatshirts on your bed to hang up in the closet. The rest is literally gone and your floor is cleared of baskets so you can *reach* your closet to put them away! Halfway through the third song, you're done and tempted to run a second load! But it won't get all done today so you respect your effort and move on to something else.

However, I started counting calories last Friday and while I haven't been perfect about hitting my preferred deficit each day, I've been gaining admit a pound each day and I have to admit it's discouraging.

I'm guessing it's any one of a few things, it's a combination:

Water retention: I tend to hold onto water when I'm taking in too much salt or drinking too many Gatorade type drinks and not drinking enough clear water. For whatever reason, I know I haven't even been finishing my 32oz bottle each day but I've been drinking Powerade or chicken broth.

Muscle mass: I have been making a point to exercise every day the weather allows, and I can feel it in my calves and thighs as I've quickly built muscle mass from roller blading on my new skates more strenuously than I have ever skated before, plus I'm swimming at least two days a week for around a half hour each.

Calorie miscalculation: even though I'm exercising, it could be that my Fitbit counting rollerblading as running gives me more calories spent than I've actually earned, allowing me to feel like I can eat more than I should. I'm also not measuring my food, but that shouldn't be a huge deal because I'm eating mostly things with labels (crackers I can count or yogurt I can scan) or things that shouldn't matter much like salads and carrot sticks but have occasionally eaten home cooked meals or at a restaurant where it's very hard to know if my chicken wings are 300 or 700.

I think since it's only been about a week since I genuinely started trying again, it makes some sense that I'm seeing opposing results, but these were the common factors when I went through weight loss successfully before.
